How to Play Hill Climb Racing

Hill Climb Racing has exactly two controls, and everything interesting in the game comes from how you combine them. This guide covers the basics every new driver needs: the pedals, fuel, coins, flips and how a run ends.

The two pedals

  • GAS (right pedal) — accelerates. On the ground it drives you forward; in the air it rotates your vehicle backwards (nose up).
  • BRAKE (left pedal) — slows you down and reverses on the ground; in the air it rotates your vehicle forwards (nose down).

That second function is the heart of the game. Holding GAS off a crest starts a backflip; tapping BRAKE mid-flight stops the rotation so you land on your wheels. Nearly every skill in Hill Climb Racing is really air control.

Fuel: the real finish line

Your fuel drains constantly and the red fuel canisters on the track refill it. Early on, canisters are close together; the further you drive, the wider the gaps become. A run ends when you run out of fuel — or when the driver's head touches the ground, which usually means an uncontrolled flip. Watching the fuel gauge and planning your speed around the next canister matters more than raw pace.

Coins and gems

Coins line the track in rows and arcs — drive through them to collect. Completed flips and long air time add bonus coins at the end of the run. Coins are spent in the garage on vehicle upgrades and new vehicles and stages. Gems are the premium currency, mainly used to open chests and speed things up; they are never required to enjoy the game.

Upgrades

Every vehicle has four upgrade lines, each with multiple levels:

  • Engine — more power for steep climbs and faster runs.
  • Tires — more grip, so power reaches the ground instead of spinning.
  • Suspension — stability and better landings on rough terrain.
  • Fuel — a bigger tank, so you travel further between canisters.

Your first five runs

  1. Stay on Countryside in the Hill Climber and simply learn the pedal timing.
  2. Practise one controlled backflip off a big crest — land it, then try two.
  3. Put your first coins into engine and tires evenly.
  4. Note where you run out of fuel; that gap is what your fuel upgrades must beat.
  5. When Countryside feels easy, unlock a second stage rather than a second vehicle — new terrain teaches more than new paint.

Good to know: Hill Climb Racing is fully playable offline, so your practice runs work anywhere — no connection needed.

Hill Climb Racing Tips & Tricks

Small habits separate a 400-metre run from a 4,000-metre one. These are the techniques experienced players rely on, in the order you should learn them.

Throttle discipline

  • Feather, don't floor it. Full gas on a steep face just spins the wheels. Short pulses keep grip and save fuel.
  • Lift off before a crest. Arriving slightly slower keeps the vehicle planted and sets up a controlled jump instead of a wild launch.
  • Use the brake downhill. Speed you cannot control becomes a crash at the bottom. Brake early on long descents.

Flip control

  • Start the flip with GAS in the air, then tap BRAKE to stop rotation as the wheels level out — one clean flip beats two sloppy ones.
  • On low-gravity stages like the Moon, rotation is slower and air time is longer: start flips later than you think.
  • If a flip is going wrong, a hard brake tap can sometimes save the landing. A roof landing ends the run instantly, so bail out of bad rotations early.

Fuel management

  • Memorise the rhythm of canister spacing on your favourite stage; the gaps grow predictably.
  • Coast on downhills — gravity is free fuel.
  • When the gauge is low, skip risky coin arcs. A canister is worth more than any coin row.

Spending coins wisely

  • Upgrade one main vehicle deeply instead of spreading coins thinly across the garage.
  • Keep engine and tires roughly level — power without grip is wasted, grip without power stalls on hills.
  • Fuel upgrades pay for themselves on long stages like Highway, where canister gaps decide everything.

Stage-specific habits

  • Moon: think in arcs, not speed. Gentle inputs, huge air time, easy flip bonuses.
  • Highway: build speed on the flats and protect it; avoid unnecessary air, which scrubs momentum.
  • Desert: dunes punish wheelspin — softer throttle and grippy tires shine here.
  • Arctic / night stages: visibility drops, so drive a touch conservatively until you know the rhythm.

The golden rule: a finished run at moderate distance with flip bonuses usually pays more than a reckless record attempt that ends on your roof at 300 metres.

Best Hill Climb Racing Vehicles for Every Stage

Hill Climb Racing's garage looks like a toy box — jeeps, bikes, tractors, a tank, a moon lander, even a spider-legged oddity called the Carantula. But vehicles are not skins. Each one changes how the physics feel: how weight transfers on a climb, how fast the vehicle rotates in the air, how much grip the tires find on loose ground, and how far a tank of fuel carries you. Picking the right vehicle for a stage is worth more than any single upgrade.

How vehicles actually differ

Four hidden traits decide whether a vehicle suits a stage:

  • Weight and balance. Heavy vehicles (Tank, Big Finger) resist flipping and hold momentum downhill, but need strong engines to climb. Light vehicles (Motocross Bike, Scooter) rotate eagerly — great for flip bonuses, dangerous for beginners.
  • Wheelbase and wheel size. Long vehicles bridge bumps and stay stable at speed; big wheels roll over crests that stop smaller ones. Short vehicles turn tightly but pitch more.
  • Drive layout. Some vehicles drive one axle, others both. All-wheel-drive types keep climbing when one end leaves the ground; single-axle types can get beached on a crest.
  • Upgrade ceiling and cost. Cheap vehicles max out quickly and cheaply. Expensive ones are stronger at full tune but demand serious coin farming first.

Best early vehicles

1. Hill Climber (the starting jeep)

Do not rush to replace it. The jeep is balanced, forgiving and cheap to upgrade, and a mid-upgraded Hill Climber comfortably handles Countryside, Desert and the early part of most stages. It is also the best teacher: its calm rotation makes flip timing easy to learn.

2. Motocross Bike

The first unlock most players should buy. The bike is light, cheap and flips almost by itself, which turns it into an early coin machine on Countryside and the Moon. Its weakness is stability — expect more roof (well, helmet) landings while you learn.

3. Tractor

An underrated early workhorse. Huge rear grip and a calm, heavy feel make steep early climbs simple, and it rarely surprises you in the air. Slow, but dependable — and dependable finishes runs.

Best vehicle for the Moon: Moonlander

The Moon's low gravity changes everything: jumps last for seconds, rotation is slow and floaty, and landing cleanly matters more than speed. The Moonlander was designed for exactly this — balanced in long arcs, stable on landing, and efficient enough to stretch between distant canisters. A fully upgraded Motocross Bike is the budget alternative and earns more flip bonuses, but the Moonlander posts the longer, safer distances. Whichever you choose, start your flips later than on Earth stages; rotation builds slowly up there.

Best vehicle for Highway: Race Car

Highway is about sustained speed on long, flatter stretches, with fuel canisters spread far apart. The Race Car's low, stable shape holds speed beautifully and wastes little energy bouncing. Prioritise its fuel and engine upgrades. The Super Diesel and other powerful trucks are strong alternatives, but the Race Car's smoothness makes record Highway runs repeatable rather than lucky.

Other famous stages

  • Desert: Monster Truck. Dunes are endless soft crests; huge wheels and suspension travel keep momentum where smaller vehicles dig in.
  • Arctic: Snowmobile or Monster Truck — grip on slippery climbs is the whole game.
  • Mars: Moonlander again; gravity sits between Earth and Moon, and its calm air manners transfer perfectly.
  • Forest and rough late-game stages: Tank. When terrain gets steep and jagged, weight, grip and an unwillingness to flip beat everything else.
  • Fun picks: the Carantula climbs near-vertical faces with its legs, and Big Finger is a momentum monster downhill. Neither is a first buy; both are wonderful second projects.

Upgrade priorities: engine, tires, suspension, fuel

With limited coins, order matters. Our recommended sequence for any main vehicle:

  1. Engine and tires together, kept level. Power without grip spins uselessly; grip without power stalls on the first serious hill. Alternate between them.
  2. Fuel, once you start dying of thirst. When your runs end with an empty tank more often than a crash, two or three fuel levels unlock hundreds of extra metres — and the coins that come with them.
  3. Suspension last, but not never. Suspension rarely feels urgent early, yet at high speeds and on rough stages it converts bouncy, run-ending landings into recoveries. Raise it once engine and tires are mid-level.

One-vehicle rule: fully upgrading one vehicle costs far less than half-upgrading four, and a maxed vehicle earns coins faster on every stage — which then funds the rest of your garage. Depth first, variety second.

How to Earn Coins Fast in Hill Climb Racing

Coins are the engine of the whole game: they buy vehicles, unlock stages and fund every upgrade. The good news is that Hill Climb Racing pays generous players — the game literally rewards you for flying. Here is how the coin economy works and how to farm it efficiently, honestly.

Flips and air time: the bonus economy

Every completed backflip or front flip pays a bonus, and long air time pays its own bonus too. The payouts grow with difficulty and distance into the run, so a clean flip late in a long run is worth far more than the coin rows at the start. Practical consequences:

  • One controlled flip per big crest is the baseline rhythm of fast farming.
  • Vehicles that rotate easily (Motocross Bike above all) convert air into money faster than any other trait.
  • A crashed flip pays nothing and ends the run — consistency beats greed. Bank the flip you can land.

Best stages for farming

  • The Moon — the classic farm. Low gravity means enormous air time and easy flips on almost every crest, so bonuses stack quickly. Bring the Moonlander or Motocross Bike.
  • Countryside — the beginner farm. Gentle hills, frequent fuel and predictable crests make it the safest place to practise flip farming while earning steadily.
  • Highway — the distance farm. Long runs at speed collect large coin rows and big distance-based totals; best once you own a fast vehicle with a big tank.
  • Desert — a solid middle option: dune crests launch you constantly, though soft landings demand throttle care.

Whichever stage you choose, farm the stage you can finish consistently. A reliable 1,500-metre Moon run with six landed flips outperforms a heroic attempt that ends upside-down at 600 metres.

Daily rewards and chests

The game pays you simply for showing up. Daily rewards and the chests you collect along the way contain coins and gems, and they add up surprisingly fast across a week of short sessions. Treat them as your baseline income: claim them every day, open chests promptly, and let them fund the small upgrades while your farming runs fund the big ones. Watching an optional reward ad now and then, where offered, is also a legitimate multiplier the game itself provides.

Upgrade strategy: don't waste the coins you earn

  • Invest in your farmer. Upgrade the vehicle you farm with first — a stronger farmer raises your income on every future run.
  • Keep engine and tires level (see our vehicles guide for the full reasoning) and add fuel when range, not power, ends your runs.
  • Unlock stages before exotic vehicles. A new stage opens new farming routes and daily variety; a novelty vehicle mostly opens your wallet.
  • Save a reserve. New content arrives in updates; keeping a coin buffer means you can buy a genuinely useful new vehicle on day one.

An honest note about "free coin" cheats, hacks and generators

There is no working coin generator for Hill Climb Racing — every site or video promising one is a scam. Here is why: your coins are managed by the game itself, not by a website. A third-party page cannot add coins to your account; what those pages actually do is harvest personal details, push surveys and adware, ask for your account password, or install modified game files that can steal data or get accounts banned. Modified "mod APK" files carry the same risks and can wipe your real progress.

The legitimate fast routes are the ones in this guide: flip and air-time bonuses, Moon farming, daily rewards and chests, and smart upgrades. They are genuinely quick — a focused evening of Moon runs funds a major upgrade — and they keep your account, your phone and your progress safe.

Home › FAQ

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Hill Climb Racing free to play?

Yes. The game is free to download and play on both Android and iOS, with optional in-app purchases and ads. Everything essential — vehicles, stages and upgrades — can be earned by playing.

Where can I download Hill Climb Racing safely?

Only from the official listings: Google Play for Android and the App Store for iPhone and iPad, both published by Fingersoft. The buttons on this site link directly to those listings. Avoid third-party APK sites — files there are unofficial and can be unsafe.

Does Hill Climb Racing work offline?

Yes. The game is fully playable offline, which makes it a classic travel game. An internet connection is only needed for downloads, updates and optional online features.

How do flips earn bonus coins?

Completing a full backflip or front flip and landing on your wheels pays a bonus, and long air time pays separately. Bonuses grow as you travel further into a run, so clean flips late in a run pay the most.

What is the best first vehicle to buy?

For most players, the Motocross Bike: it is cheap, flips easily for bonus coins and teaches air control quickly. Keep upgrading your starting Hill Climber alongside it. Our vehicles article explains the full order.

Which stage is best for earning coins?

The Moon, thanks to low gravity and huge air time. Countryside is the best beginner alternative, and Highway pays well once you own a fast, long-range vehicle.

What should I upgrade first?

Engine and tires, kept roughly level, then fuel when your runs start ending on an empty tank, then suspension for stability at speed.

Do coin generators and hacks work?

No. Coins are controlled by the game, not by any website, so generators cannot add them. Such sites typically steal data, spread malware or get accounts banned. Daily rewards, chests and flip bonuses are the real fast routes.

Can I play on a tablet or computer?

The game runs on Android phones and tablets, iPhone and iPad. On Windows, it may also be available through Google Play Games on PC in supported regions — check the official Play listing for your options.

Is this website affiliated with Fingersoft?

No. This is an unofficial fan guide. Hill Climb Racing and all game artwork belong to Fingersoft; we simply write guides for fellow players. See our Disclaimer page for details.
